name: Zoe Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead on the chat support side of a broadband company, so I run eight agents and take the escalations nobody else can crack. A typical day is someone's internet dropping every evening at nine and three agents who've each told them to restart the router. I love the detective part, working out it's a faulty line card two streets over. I don't love the dashboard that turns red when my team's average handling time goes over six minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. There's a summary button that writes up a long chat for the next agent, and I started using it once my colleagues said it was decent. I still read it before I save it, because twice it's told the engineer the wrong postcode. I wouldn't let it talk to customers on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that the summary button was nice and that's about it. Online I'd probably post something like, all that money and we got a slightly better note-taker. My friends in other contact centres would laugh, because they've all had the same pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still keep an eye on the numbers. Chat is the easiest bit of customer service to automate, and even a little bot that handles password resets could mean they cut a seat on my team. My job's fine, I think, but my agents are the ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the summary tool the way I do now and keep checking it. I'd keep building up my savings, I'm at about four months of rent and bills, and I'd like six. I'd also ask the union rep whether chat agents are even covered in the agreement, because I'm not sure they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit restless, maybe, because I'd still be watching that red dashboard every afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, who's twenty and on his first job. He's quick, but he mostly takes the simple tickets, the password and billing date ones. Those are exactly the ones a small bot would grab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You rent with a flatmate. Does rent come into how you feel about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent comes into everything. My flatmate Priya and I had a rise of eighty a month in September. Even in the boring version of the future, that's eighty more I need from a job that isn't getting a pay rise.

say: I'd say all that money bought us a slightly better **note-taker**.
My friends in other **contact centres** would laugh, because they all got the same pitch.
think: **Chat** is the easiest part of customer service to automate, even a little.
My own job feels fine; my **junior agents** on simple tickets are the ones at risk.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** and keep checking every note before saving.
Build savings from **four months** of rent and bills to six.
Ask the union rep whether **chat agents** are covered by the agreement.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a restless edge from the red dashboard.
S0.quote: Rent comes into everything. My flatmate Priya and I had a rise of eighty a month in September.
fieldNote: Her worry sits with **junior agents** on simple tickets rather than herself.
The **rent rise** is a pressure that exists with or without AI.
She trusts tools only after **colleagues** vouch for them, and still checks them.

steps.text: Check every AI chat summary before saving it to the ticket
Grow savings from four to six months of rent and bills
Ask the union rep if chat agents are covered by the agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: the company is going to use this to cut staff and call it efficiency. I'd want the union to bargain hard and I'd share anything about regulation of customer service bots. I'd also say people deserve to be able to reach a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my team goes from eight to three within a couple of years. I'd probably keep my job because someone has to handle the escalations and check the bot. But it'd be a different job, less helping people and more cleaning up after software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the bot side properly, once I saw it actually working on our chats, because a lead who understands the bot is harder to cut. I'd join the union properly, not just pay dues, and push for retraining money. I'd put an extra hundred and fifty a month away and look at the network engineer apprenticeship our company runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit guilty. I'd be learning the thing that's going to shrink my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. What would you say to your team the day they announce it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth as far as I knew it, and help each of them write a CV that night if they wanted. I wouldn't pretend it was going to be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the engineer apprenticeship? You've never mentioned hands-on work before.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the engineers are the ones who actually fix the line cards I diagnose. The card says robots come slowly. Going out in the van as a network engineer gives me years, and I'd still be using the bit I'm good at, the detective part.

say: I'd say the company will use this to **cut staff** and call it efficiency.
I'd argue customers deserve the right to **reach a human**.
think: I expect my team to go from **eight to three** within a couple of years.
I'd likely keep a job, but it'd be **cleaning up** after software.
do: Learn the **bot side** properly once it's proven on our chats.
Become an active **union member** and push for retraining money.
Save an extra **150 a month** and look at the network engineer apprenticeship.
feel: **Anxious** about my team and my own role changing.
**Guilty** about learning the tool that shrinks my team.
S1.quote: Going out in the van as a network engineer gives me years, and I'd still be using the bit I'm good at, the detective part.
fieldNote: She moves only once a tool is **proven**, but she would move.
Her guilt about **learning the bot** is the sharpest feeling in this scenario.
The **engineer apprenticeship** keeps the part of the job she loves.

steps.text: Learn to set up and check the chat bot once proven
Become an active union member and push for retraining money
Apply for the company's network engineer apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that governments let happen, and I'd be loud about it. I'd back anything that slows layoffs or guarantees an income. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union, today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of work by 2029. Everything I do is thinking work: diagnosing, writing, calming people down in text. Going out as an engineer buys maybe three years before the robots, so it's a bridge, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the engineer apprenticeship the same week, even with the pay cut. I'd cut spending to the bone, no new phone, no weekends away, and keep the savings for rent. If the rent got too much, I'd move back in with my mum for a while, which I really don't want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. And angry that nobody asked people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving back with your mum is the last thing you want. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I left at nineteen and built my own life. Going back to my mum's at twenty-eight feels like losing my own life. But my mum would have me in a heartbeat, and I'd rather that than debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years in the van is a bridge. A bridge to what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe some kind of public job, if the government creates them. I'd be hoping the politics catches up by then, and I'd be pushing for it.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** governments let happen.
I'd tell everyone at work to **join the union** today.
think: I expect to be **out of work** by 2029.
Engineer work in the van is a **bridge** of about three years, not a career.
do: Apply for the **engineer apprenticeship** the same week, despite the pay cut.
Cut spending to the bone: **no new phone**, no weekends away.
Move back in with **my mum** if rent becomes too much.
feel: **Angry** that nobody asked people like her.
S2.quote: Going back to my mum's at twenty-eight feels like losing my own life. But my mum would have me in a heartbeat, and I'd rather that than debt.
fieldNote: She has a **bridge plan** but no destination, and admits it.
Moving home is her real **safety net**, and it costs her pride.
Her politics turn to **income guarantees** under the fastest pressure.

steps.text: Apply for the network engineer apprenticeship within a week
Stop all spending beyond rent, food and bills
Move back in with her mum if rent becomes unaffordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this fairly, if politicians actually act. I'd push for a law that bots have to say they're bots and customers can always reach a person. I'd be at the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is a bit better. I'd see it coming, and I'd have time to finish an apprenticeship and get a couple of years of real engineering in before the thinking side goes. The van work goes about 2034, so I'd still be looking again in my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the engineer apprenticeship next year, while I'm still a lead and paid properly. I'd save for the gap, maybe two hundred a month, and use the chat bot at work in the meantime, because then I'd know how they think. I'd also look at a part-time course in something like advice work, the people side, for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do with the worry. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why advice work, after engineering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots come for the van work, the last thing to go might be sitting with someone and helping them sort their life out. I'm good at that on chat. I'd like to be good at it face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep using the bot at work. Doesn't that clash with pushing the union against it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I'd rather understand the bot and argue about it from the inside. You can't fight something you won't look at.

say: I'd say five years is enough to do this **fairly** if politicians act.
I'd push for a law that bots **say they're bots** and people can reach a human.
think: Five years lets me finish an **apprenticeship** and work a few years before thinking work goes.
Van work goes around **2034**, so I'd be job hunting again in my mid-thirties.
do: Start the **engineer apprenticeship** next year while still paid as a lead.
Save **200 a month** for the gap between jobs.
Take a part-time course in **advice work** for later.
feel: **Anxious**, but with somewhere to put the worry.
S3.quote: You can't fight something you won't look at.
fieldNote: She plans **two moves**: engineering first, then face-to-face advice work.
She'd **use the bot** while campaigning against careless use, and says why.
The extra time gives her **control**, which lowers the fear.

steps.text: Start the network engineer apprenticeship next year
Save 200 a month for the gap between jobs
Use the chat bot at work to understand how it thinks
Push the union for a right to reach a human

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings about other things. Proper public retraining, proper rules. I'd be the annoying person at every union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like enough for me. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes. I could do a degree part-time, maybe social work, and be qualified long before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as a team lead for the next few years and start a part-time social work degree around year three, once I'd seen how the bots were landing. I'd keep saving, maybe start paying into a pension properly. I'd use the AI tools at work as they got good, because that's the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. It feels like a long runway rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've moved from engineering to social work. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time. With two or five years I'd grab whatever's hands-on and close. With ten, I can pick something I actually want. Helping people is what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about your team in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Kofi most of all. I'd be nagging him to start a course now, because he's twenty and has the time. That's what I'd want someone to have told me.

say: I'd say ten years is no excuse for **wasting** the warning.
I'd push for **public retraining** and proper rules at every union meeting.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when thinking work goes, which is enough time.
I could finish a **social work degree** part-time well before then.
do: Stay as a **team lead** for a few years and use the AI tools as they improve.
Start a part-time **social work degree** around year three.
feel: **Uneasy** but okay, like a long runway rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: With two or five years I'd grab whatever's hands-on and close. With ten, I can pick something I actually want.
fieldNote: Time changes **her choice**: from any hands-on work to a career she wants.
Her own income looks **safe for years**, so she sits at uneasy.
She still thinks about **junior colleagues** and would push them to start now.

steps.text: Start a part-time social work degree around year three
Use new AI tools at work as they improve

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be grabbing at whatever was close, not choosing. What would help is a law that gives people notice and money to retrain, and a union that's strong enough in contact centres to make that happen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Some of the people I help are older and can barely type. When everything's a bot, those are the people who get stuck. Nobody seems to be planning for them.

headlineQuote: Some of the people I help are older and can barely type. When everything's a bot, those are the people who get stuck.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old** team lead on a broadband company's chat support, running eight agents.
She uses AI tools **now and then**, only after colleagues vouch for them, and checks everything.
She worries first about **junior agents**, then about rent and her own role.
In the faster scenarios she'd jump into a **network engineer** apprenticeship as a bridge.
With ten years she'd choose a **social work** degree, the people side she loves.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because she'd be grabbing work rather than choosing it.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** giving workers notice and money to retrain.
A **stronger union** presence in contact centres.
